model: GPT-6 family via Codex; exact deployment unavailable
reading_coverage: Read complete frozen manuscript text, pages 1–10: abstract, Sections 1–6, equations, experiments and references. Verified PDF SHA-256.
Visually inspected pages 4 and 5 for Equations (2)–(8), candidate inclusion and approximation claims; page 7 for objective and setup; pages 8 and 9 for Figure 1 and Tables 1–2.

Retrospective ICLR 2017 assessment. No source code, raw logs, supplementary material or external cited papers inspected; no historical human reviews or other reviewer outputs consulted. Missing access is not itself treated as a defect.
Competence: relevant familiarity with supervised memory retrieval, approximate search and truncated softmax training. Historical novelty and cited search guarantees were not independently verified.
Cross-examination: read only the assigned opposite EUCN frozen review and its two-check incoming package; recorded one response to each check without external or historical outcome consultation.
score_reason: 5: Marginally below acceptance threshold. Approximate retrieval with supervised query learning is coherent, and exact-search experiments report a useful within-setting accuracy observation, not a replicated causal mechanism. Reduced fact access is supported, but end-to-end training and inference benefits remain unresolved at the reported accuracy losses. Table 2 shows convergence differences among approximate configurations, not a demonstrated excess over full softmax. Gradient concentration and bias reduction remain hypotheses rather than established explanations. Together these leave the central speed–accuracy claim and operating conditions insufficiently characterized. A measured useful large-memory operating point with appropriately bounded claims could materially strengthen the paper; multiple memory sizes are desirable rather than an inflexible prerequisite. No theorem, contemporary baseline or state-of-the-art QA result is required.
change_reason: Score unchanged after one bounded cross-examination. I clarified that the exact-selection gain is a reported within-setting result, and narrowed the convergence-cost interpretation to avoid implying that Table 2 establishes extra epochs relative to full softmax. These corrections preserve the positive observation and the central unresolved practical scalability concern, so they do not change the threshold judgment.

evidence.claim: The reader gives a coherent supervised mechanism for learning queries against a fixed searchable memory.
evidence.observation: The model retrieves an inner-product candidate subset, normalizes on that subset and inserts the correct fact during training. Fixed memory embeddings keep the search index compatible with the representation being queried. The text distinguishes exact from approximate retrieval and explicitly leaves memory updates to future work.
evidence.consequence: This is an implementable bridge between sparse retrieval and differentiable query learning with an explicit supervision assumption.
evidence.scope: Known supporting facts and fixed memory; not evidence for unsupervised or writable-memory training.
evidence.would_change_judgment: An inconsistency between candidate construction and the objective would remove this strength.

evidence.claim: The exact-search experiment gives meaningful evidence that candidate restriction can improve this QA model.
evidence.location: Section 5.4, p. 7; Table 1 and Figure 1, p. 8.
evidence.observation: The shared fixed-TransE/bag-of-words model reports 59.5% test accuracy with full softmax and 62.2% with exact 10-MIPS, declining toward 59.6% as K reaches 1000. Figure 1 shows similar epoch-scale convergence. The authors disclose minibatch candidate unions: the average 10-MIPS training softmax size is 1290.
evidence.consequence: The systematic reported trend establishes an interesting restricted-objective effect worth investigating.
evidence.scope: Single-dataset exact-MIPS results, not a runtime speedup or a universal ordering of attention mechanisms.
evidence.would_change_judgment: Instability across replications would reduce this strength; independent confirmation would increase it.

evidence.claim: The scalable-training claim lacks sufficient computational accounting and scaling evidence.
evidence.location: Section 3.1, p. 5, after Equation (8); Section 5.5, p. 8; Tables 1–2.
evidence.observation: The statement that each read requires only K centroid dot products omits scoring retrieved memory candidates for the final softmax. Section 5.5 associates about 20,000 accessed facts versus 108,442 with a 5X speedup, without reporting hardware, elapsed training/inference time, index construction costs or multiple memory sizes. Table 2 shows 16–68 convergence epochs across similar-access configurations.
evidence.consequence: Reduced fact access is supported, but end-to-end speed and scalable learning do not follow from this count alone. Search overhead and extra epochs may change the benefit.
evidence.scope: Evidence for computational scaling and speed; not a claim that approximate search cannot be faster.
evidence.remedy: Report search, softmax and total elapsed costs, convergence time and index overhead at multiple memory sizes; separate centroid and candidate scoring.
evidence.would_change_judgment: A measured favorable time–accuracy frontier would materially improve the score.

evidence.claim: Gradient concentration and bias reduction are not isolated by the reported evidence.
evidence.location: Section 3, p. 4, after Equation (4); Section 3.1, p. 5; Section 5.5 and Table 2.
evidence.observation: The paper says high-score cells receive the strongest gradients and candidate sharing or sampled clusters reduces gradient bias. For the stated NLL objective, the query gradient is a model-weighted mean of fact vectors minus the gold vector; truncation changes both normalization and that vector mean. Small individual probabilities alone do not imply negligible aggregate effects. No gradient discrepancy, captured mass, retrieval recall or matched-size candidate control is reported. Table 2 measures accuracy and epochs rather than bias.
evidence.consequence: The empirical gains are useful, but they do not establish why the strategies work or that they reliably move gradients toward the full-softmax gradient.
evidence.scope: Mechanistic interpretation, not validity of the algorithm; no theorem is demanded.
evidence.remedy: Frame these as hypotheses or measure gradient discrepancy and retrieval recall, with matched-size alternative candidate controls.
evidence.would_change_judgment: Evidence connecting selection to gradient quality and convergence would strengthen the explanatory contribution.

evidence.claim: The demonstrated operating range is narrower than the general recommendation for K-MIPS attention.
evidence.observation: Experiments use one 108,442-fact SimpleQuestions memory, fixed TransE vectors, a bag-of-words query and gold-fact supervision. The 10M/12M fact databases are explicitly omitted to permit full-softmax comparisons. Best approximate accuracy is 53.1%, versus 59.5% full softmax and 62.2% exact 10-MIPS. Section 5.4 nevertheless recommends K-MIPS whenever possible, and the motivation reaches arbitrary fact structures/modalities.
evidence.consequence: The data establish a particular access-count/accuracy tradeoff rather than a general replacement rule. The scalable variant retains a 6.4-point gap to full softmax, making its useful regime especially important.
evidence.scope: Transfer and practical significance of approximation; the explicitly non-SOTA aim is reasonable.
evidence.remedy: Narrow the recommendation and provide a larger-memory or second-setting experiment, or a recall/accuracy frontier establishing a useful operating regime.
evidence.would_change_judgment: Consistent favorable tradeoffs beyond this fixed-memory setup would strengthen significance.

evidence.claim: The approximate-reader comparison lacks details and variability estimates needed for reliable replication.
evidence.observation: Optimizer, learning rate, batch size and embedding dimensions are given, but numerical U and augmentation m, selected-cluster counts, a complete sampling probability rule and chosen hash/tree settings are not reported. No run counts or variation estimates accompany the close 52.8% versus 53.1% best configurations.
evidence.consequence: The broad approximate/exact gap is visible, but preferred approximation settings, tuning fairness and the reliability of small differences are difficult to establish.
evidence.scope: Specification and stability, not evidence of improper implementation or tuning.
evidence.remedy: Provide complete search and sampling settings, tuning budgets and repeated-run variation.
evidence.would_change_judgment: Complete specification and replication would raise confidence; changed rankings would alter interpretation.

evidence.claim: Historical novelty is provisional based on the manuscript’s own positioning.
evidence.observation: The manuscript credits prior MIPS transformations and clustering, describes the contribution as using retrieval during reader learning, and distinguishes independent sparse memory access by its fixed external-KB setting. I have not independently inspected those contemporaneous sources.
evidence.consequence: The integration may be a useful 2017 contribution, but no decisive external novelty objection or priority claim is verified here.
evidence.scope: Historical priority and distinctions from cited contemporaneous work; no 2026 baselines applied.
evidence.remedy: Externally compare objective, support supervision and fixed-memory assumptions with the closest cited 2016 work.
evidence.would_change_judgment: Verified central overlap could lower novelty; a clear contemporaneous distinction would strengthen it.

challenges.challenge: Confirmed within the stated scope: Table 1 (p. 8) reports 59.5% for full softmax, 62.2% for exact 10-MIPS and 59.6% for 1000-MIPS, with the minibatch-union size explicitly given as 1290 for 10-MIPS. Figure 1 supports comparable convergence in epochs. From a utility-focused perspective this is a meaningful positive result even though exact search saves no asymptotic retrieval work. I would retain the strength but read “establishes an interesting restricted-objective effect” as a reported within-setting effect rather than a replicated mechanism: Section 5.4 changes the candidate objective, Table 1 supplies no variability, and the evidence does not isolate gradient concentration as its cause. Your existing single-setting and no-runtime caveats are sound.
challenges.response: Accepted as a wording clarification: the 59.5% to 62.2% comparison and the trend across K in Table 1, p. 8, establish a reported within-setting observation, not a replicated causal mechanism. Section 5.4, p. 7, changes the normalized candidate objective and shares candidates across the minibatch. I retain this positive evidence while interpreting “restricted-objective effect” descriptively; it does not demonstrate gradient concentration as the cause. This matches the separate mechanistic limitation in digr-e4.

challenges.challenge: Confirmed: Section 3.1 (p. 5, after Eq. 8) counts centroid dot products, while Eq. 4 (p. 4) still requires scoring selected memory vectors. Section 5.5 (p. 8) associates roughly 20,000 fact accesses with 5X speedup but supplies no elapsed-cost table; Table 2 (p. 9) gives 16–68 epochs. This supports the major concern about practical time-to-accuracy, not a finding that the method is slower. One qualification: variation in Table 2 is among approximate configurations, so it cannot itself establish extra convergence epochs relative to the full-softmax baseline. The useful empirical revision is a measured end-to-end time/accuracy frontier; multiple memory sizes would strengthen the broad scalability claim but need not become an inflexible checklist if one clearly useful large-memory operating point is established.
challenges.response: Accepted. Table 2, p. 9, compares approximate configurations; its 16–68 epoch spread does not demonstrate more epochs than full softmax. My reference to “extra epochs” is therefore limited to possible configuration-dependent total costs, not an observed penalty relative to the full-softmax baseline. Reduced fact access remains established by Section 5.5, p. 8, while practical runtime benefit remains unresolved. The missing candidate-scoring cost after the centroid count on p. 5 supports the accounting concern. Multiple memory sizes would help establish scaling, but a clearly useful, fully costed large-memory operating point together with appropriately narrowed claims could also materially improve the judgment; this is not an inflexible experimental checklist.
